extracted.intended_audience: federal agency officials, OPM/MSPB/OSC practitioners, federal HR/legal counsel, and rulemaking commenters interested in civil-service adverse-action and appointment-exception law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and regulatory standards governing which federal positions are excepted from civil-service protections (e.g., adverse-action rights), how those exceptions are created and communicated, and related hiring and classification rules referenced in a rulemaking response.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2) pre-appointment determination requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For the section 7511(b)(2) exclusion to be effective as to a particular individual, the appropriate official must designate the position in question as confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating before the individual is appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case law (e.g., Thompson v. Dep't of Justice; King v. Briggs; Owens v. Dep't of Health & Human Servs.) emphasizes that a determination under 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2) is not adequate unless it is made before appointment and, where relevant, communicated to the appointee. In the absence of a timely determination and communication, section 7511(b)(2) does not limit adverse-action rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception at 7511(b)(2) requires appropriate decisionmaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (b)(2) also specifies who may make the determination for positions that Congress itself excepts from the competitive service (see 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2)(C)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The determination that a position is confidential/policy-making/etc. must be made by the appropriate person or entity identified in the statute (e.g., President, OPM, or Congress when Congress excepts a position). Example: U.S. Trustee position discussed in Stanley v. Dep't of Justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception is not self-executing; statutory/administrative action required
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision is not self-executing: the statute outlines categories for exemption rather than creating automatic exemptions for positions simply because of their character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments and legislative history indicate Congress intended that some employees could be 'policymaking,' but OPM and legal interpretation treat the exception as operative only where the statute/regulations and designated authorities have acted to except the position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excepted service definition (5 U.S.C. 2103(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of title 5, 'the excepted service consists of those civil service positions which are not in the competitive service or the Senior Executive Service.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory definition distinguishes excepted service positions from competitive service and SES positions and determines applicability of various protections and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: SES exclusion from 7511(b)(2) exception and at-will status of noncareer SES
rubrics_metrics.description: The exception at 5 U.S.C. 7511(b)(2) does not apply to the Senior Executive Service. The Subchapter on adverse actions establishes the at-will status of noncareer SES by defining 'employee' for purposes of that Subchapter as career employees (see sections 7541-7543).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the excepted service does not include the SES (see 5 U.S.C. 2103(a)), the policymaking/confidential exception in 7511(b)(2) is inapplicable to SES, and noncareer SES do not have the chapter 75 protections applicable to career employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule A/B/C transition rule (employee status retention)
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee in the competitive service at the time his position is first listed under Schedule A, B, or C remains in the competitive service while he occupies that position (Revision of Regulations, 33 FR 12402-08; 5 CFR 212.401(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory history and current regulation preserve incumbent competitive-service status despite subsequent reclassification of the position into an excepted schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule C positions are political appointees excluded from 7511(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schedule C positions (positions of a confidential or policy‑determining character) are political appointees who are specifically excluded from coverage under section 7511(b) of title 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history (H.R. Rep. No. 101-328) and agency practice treat Schedule C positions as excepted from adverse-action protections applicable to career employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veterans' preference must be applied to excepted-service hiring as feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3320 of title 5 requires appointing authorities hiring individuals into the excepted service to use the same procedures described in sections 3308 to 3318 of title 5 to effectuate veterans' preference; OPM's part 302 regulations provide the means to meet that requirement and allow limited exemptions only where compliance is essentially impossible (e.g., attorney positions for which Congress has forbidden examination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even for discrete excepted-service positions and limited exemptions under 5 CFR 302.101(c), veterans' preference must still be applied 'as far as administratively feasible.'

rubrics_metrics.name: MSPB and OSC authorities and threshold showings
rubrics_metrics.description: MSPB has specific adjudicative and enforcement authority upon the satisfaction of threshold showings that an employee has established appeal rights; OSC has specific and limited investigative and prosecutorial authority (see 5 U.S.C. 1103(a)(5)(A) and 5 U.S.C. 1213-1216).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and litigants should recognize the separate roles and statutory thresholds for MSPB and OSC when assessing adjudicative or enforcement avenues related to adverse actions or Hatch Act matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of 'political appointee' for some statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain statutes define 'political appointee' as 'any employee who occupies a position which has been excepted from the competitive service by reason of its confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character' (e.g., 6 U.S.C. 349(d)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory definition is used across multiple statutes to distinguish career employees from political appointees for purposes such as exceptions from protections and applicability of certain statutes (e.g., Hatch Act notifications referencing confidential/policy-making language).

rubrics_metrics.name: APA procedural parity for rule amendments/repeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies under the Administrative Procedure Act must 'use the same procedures when they amend or repeal a rule as they used to issue the rule in the first instance' (Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Ass'n, 575 U.S. 92, 101 (2015)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When changing rules that affect civil-service classifications or employee rights, agencies should follow the same notice-and-comment and procedural steps as when the rule was originally promulgated, unless another statute provides otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/regulatory citations inform interpretation of current rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Longstanding regulations, executive orders, and historical practices (e.g., revisions at 33 FR 12402; E.O. 10440, E.O. 10577; multiple CFR provisions) are used to interpret the application and limits of exceptions and employee rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory history and precedent (including agency guides and past executive orders) are relevant interpretive tools when determining whether positions are excepted, what procedures apply, and how protections like veterans' preference and appeal rights have been treated over time.
